scenarios.title: Scenario 5 — Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenarios.domains: D4 Prompt Engineering · D3 Claude Code Configuration · D2 Tool Design & MCP
scenarios.brief: A travel-booking company runs Claude Code headlessly in GitHub Actions on a Kotlin and TypeScript repository. Jobs: a pull-request review that posts inline comments, an autofix job for failing builds, test generation for new endpoints, and a weekly dependency-risk report across all modules. The review job connects to an internal MCP server for code search and API guidelines. CLAUDE.md and .claude/ are committed.

scenarios.title: Scenario 6 — Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.domains: D4 Prompt Engineering · D1 Agentic Architecture · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: An insurance broker extracts data from certificates of insurance and policy schedules sent by about sixty carriers. Some arrive as text PDFs, others as OCR'd scans. Claude returns insured name, carrier, policy number, coverage lines with limits and deductibles, and effective and expiry dates through a tool with a JSON schema. Pydantic validates each result before it posts to the broker's system. An Agent SDK coordinator handles multi-document submissions; account assistants review exceptions.

questions.question: A senior engineer wrote the team's review criteria into her own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Her local reviews follow them well. The CI review job and her teammates' sessions ignore them. The criteria apply to every file in the repository, in every language. Where should the criteria live so that the CI job and every developer load them on every review?

options.t: Commit them as a .claude/rules/ file whose paths: globs cover the Kotlin and TypeScript sources.
options.why: Runner-up. Committed and shared, and right for conventions tied to certain file types. These criteria apply to every file, and a path-scoped rule loads only when matching files are in play.

options.t: Commit them as docs/review-criteria.md and reference that file in the CI job's -p prompt.
options.why: Incorrect. CI would get them, but developers' sessions never load a file that only the CI prompt mentions.

options.t: Commit them to the project CLAUDE.md at the repository root, under a review criteria section.
options.why: Correct. Project CLAUDE.md is shared through version control and loads in every session, local or headless.

options.t: Commit them as a project skill in .claude/skills/review/ that CI and developers invoke.
options.why: Incorrect. Shared, but skills load on demand. Any session that doesn't invoke the skill skips the criteria.

questions.decider: The criteria apply to every file, so they belong in the always-loaded project CLAUDE.md; if they applied only to one file type spread across directories, a .claude/rules/ file with paths: would win.
questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md is personal and never reaches teammates or CI. Universal standards for a repository go in the committed project CLAUDE.md; path-scoped rules are for conventions tied to particular files.

eli5.question: Her rules work for her and nobody else. Where should they live? The clue is: the criteria apply to every file in the repository, in every language. So this is about who gets the file, and how widely it applies.
eli5.answer: Think of a note on your own fridge versus a notice on the office wall. Only you see the fridge note (the user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md). The wall notice is seen by everyone who walks in (the project CLAUDE.md, committed to the repo). CI and teammates clone the repo, so they only see the wall. Because the rules cover every file, they go on the main wall, not on a sign above one desk. Rule: shared standards for the whole repo go in the committed project CLAUDE.md.
options: Runner-up. A rules file with paths: is a sign over certain desks. Great for test-file rules; these rules are for every file.
Naming the file in the CI prompt reaches CI only. Developers' sessions never see it.
Correct. The committed project file reaches CI and every developer, every session.
A skill is a recipe card someone has to pull out. These rules should be on the wall all the time.

deep.premise: You'd think the problem is CI, since that's where it shows up. But her teammates miss the rules too. The real issue is scope: a file in her home folder belongs to her alone. Once you move it into the repo, the remaining choice is how widely it applies, and "every file" means the always-loaded project file.

questions.question: The project CLAUDE.md holds a single line, @docs/testing-standards.md, meant to pull in the team's testing rules. The CI test generator keeps writing tests that break those rules. A developer reproduces the problem in a local session. Nobody has yet checked whether the imported file is loaded at all. What should the developer do first?

options.t: Run /memory in that session and check whether the standards file is listed as loaded.
options.why: Correct. It is the built-in way to see which memory files loaded, and it separates "not loaded" from "loaded and ignored".

options.t: Add two finished tests that follow the rules to the generator's prompt as worked examples.
options.why: Runner-up. Few-shot examples are the right fix once the rules are confirmed loaded and output still drifts. Until then, they may hide a broken import.

options.t: Ask Claude in that session to quote the testing rules it was given, and compare them with the file.
options.why: Incorrect. A diagnostic idea, but the model's account of its own context is unreliable; it may paraphrase or invent rules.

options.t: Paste the rules inline in place of the @import line, then rerun the generator to compare.
options.why: Incorrect. An experiment by changing config. It gives up the modular import and still doesn't show what was loaded.

questions.decider: Nobody knows whether the imported file loads, so verifying with /memory comes first; if it were confirmed loaded, adding example tests would be the next step.
questions.explanation: When guidance seems ignored, first confirm what Claude Code actually loaded. /memory lists the loaded memory files; only after that do you choose between fixing the import and improving the prompt.

eli5.question: The generator breaks rules that should come in through an import. What do you do first? The clue is: nobody has checked whether the imported file is loaded at all.
eli5.answer: Think of a cook who ignores a recipe card. First check the card is actually pinned on the board before you retrain the cook. /memory shows which memory files Claude Code loaded (the board). If the testing file is missing, fix the import. If it's there and still ignored, then add examples. Rule: when instructions seem ignored, check they were loaded before changing anything.
options: Correct. A direct look at what's loaded tells you which fix you need.
Runner-up. Showing finished tests helps when the rules are loaded but followed loosely. We don't know that yet.
Asking Claude what it was told is unreliable; it can paraphrase or make rules up.
Changing the config to see what happens is a guess, and you lose the tidy import.

deep.premise: It's tempting to treat this as a prompting problem: Claude ignored the rules, so show it better examples. But there are two different causes that look identical from outside. Either the rules never reached the context, or they arrived and were ignored. Only the second is a prompting problem.

questions.trap: More context or reasoning instead of structure
questions.question: The review job runs claude -p and asks Claude to end its reply with a JSON block of findings. A script cuts out the block and posts each finding as an inline comment. On some runs Claude adds a sentence after the block, and the script posts nothing. The script needs a file, line, severity and message for every finding. Which change fixes this most reliably?

options.t: Add two complete sample replies to the prompt, each ending in a correctly placed findings block.
options.why: Runner-up. Few-shot examples make output more consistent, and would be the right step if people read the reply and only its layout varied. A script needs a contract, not a likelier layout.

options.t: Define a report_findings tool with the findings schema and force it with tool_choice.
options.why: Incorrect. That is the right pattern on the Messages API. This job calls the Claude Code CLI, which offers its own flags for structured output.

options.t: Have the script rerun the job with the parse error appended whenever it finds no block.
options.why: Incorrect. Retry-with-feedback recovers some runs but pays for a second review and keeps the fragile text format.

options.t: Run the CLI with --output-format json and a --json-schema for the findings array.
options.why: Correct. The CLI then returns machine-parseable output that matches the schema, with the required fields for each inline comment.

questions.decider: A script consumes the output through the CLI, so the CLI's --output-format json with --json-schema wins; if people read the reply and only consistency mattered, examples would be enough.
questions.explanation: In CI, Claude Code's -p mode plus --output-format json and --json-schema gives findings a script can parse. Asking for JSON in prose, even with examples, leaves the format to chance.

eli5.question: A script breaks when Claude adds chatter after the JSON. How do you fix it for good? The clue is: a script, not a person, reads every finding and needs exact fields.
eli5.answer: Think of a form with labelled boxes versus a letter that says "please put the answers at the bottom". A machine can read the form every time. --output-format json with --json-schema is the form: the Claude Code CLI returns fields that match your schema. Examples in the prompt make a tidy letter more likely, but not certain. Rule: when code reads the output in CI, use the CLI's JSON output and schema flags.
options: Runner-up. Examples make the format more likely, which is fine when people read it. A script needs a guaranteed shape.
Forcing a tool is the API way to get structured output. This job runs the CLI, which has its own flags for it.
Retrying costs a second run and keeps the fragile format.
Correct. The CLI hands the script schema-shaped JSON.

deep.premise: You'd think the fix is to ask more clearly or show the format. But output read by a program needs a contract, not a habit. The Claude Code CLI already has that contract: JSON output validated against a schema you pass in. The API's tool-use pattern is the same idea at a different layer.

questions.question: The review job's MCP server has a search_docs tool over the team's API guidelines. Before judging a diff, the reviewer calls it many times with broad queries. Those calls are an attempt to learn which guideline documents exist and how they are organised. Most of them return nothing useful. Which change best cuts these calls?

options.t: Move the doc lookups into an Explore subagent that hands back a short summary to the reviewer.
options.why: Incorrect. An Explore subagent keeps verbose output out of the main context, but it still makes the same blind calls.

options.t: Publish the documents' titles and section outline as an MCP resource read at the start of a run.
options.why: Correct. A resource exposes the catalog directly, so the reviewer knows what exists without probing.

options.t: Expand the search_docs description with its input format, sample queries and the topics it covers.
options.why: Runner-up. Better descriptions fix wrong or vague tool use. Here the tool is used correctly; the reviewer needs a map of the content, not a better label.

options.t: Split search_docs into one tool per documentation area, each with its own focused description.
options.why: Incorrect. Purpose-specific tools help selection between overlapping tools. More tools to probe does not show what exists.

questions.decider: The calls exist only to discover which documents there are, which a resource catalog answers; if the reviewer were misusing or mis-selecting the tool, a fuller description would win.
questions.explanation: MCP resources expose content catalogs such as doc hierarchies so an agent can see what exists without exploratory tool calls. Tool descriptions fix how a tool is chosen and used, not what content exists.

eli5.question: The reviewer keeps searching just to find out what documents exist. How do you stop that? The clue is: the calls are an attempt to learn which guideline documents exist and how they are organised.
eli5.answer: Think of walking into a library and shouting topics at the librarian, versus reading the catalogue by the door. An MCP resource is the catalogue: content the reviewer can read up front, like a list of documents and sections. Then searches become targeted. Rule: if the agent is probing to learn what exists, publish a catalog as a resource.
options: A helper can do the probing out of sight, but it still probes blindly.
Correct. Hand over the catalogue and the blind searching stops.
Runner-up. A clearer label helps when the tool is misused. Here the tool works; the reviewer lacks a map.
More search tools give more places to probe, not a list of what exists.

deep.premise: You'd think lots of useless tool calls means a badly described tool. But look at what the calls are for. The reviewer isn't confused about the tool; it is trying to learn what content exists. That is a catalog problem, and MCP has a primitive for catalogs: resources.

questions.question: The review job's MCP server offers find_usages. It resolves every caller of a function across modules, including calls made through interfaces. The reviewer still runs Grep on function names and misses the interface calls. The tool's description reads only "Find usages." When the reviewer does call it, the results are correct. What is the most effective first step?

options.t: Add a project CLAUDE.md rule: for callers of a function, use find_usages, not Grep.
options.why: Runner-up. A project instruction is a reasonable nudge and would be worth adding if the description were already full. The description is the primary selection signal, and here it is two words.

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook that redirects Grep calls on symbol names to find_usages instead.
options.why: Incorrect. Deterministic, but brittle: deciding which Grep patterns are symbol lookups is guesswork, and it overrides legitimate text searches.

options.t: Rewrite the find_usages description: what it resolves, sample inputs, and when to use it over Grep.
options.why: Correct. Descriptions are how the model picks tools. A two-word description gives it no reason to prefer the MCP tool over Grep.

options.t: Rename find_usages to find_all_callers, a name stating what the tool resolves.
options.why: Incorrect. Purpose-specific naming helps, but a name can't carry inputs, interface coverage or when to prefer it; the description stays two words.

questions.decider: The description is only two words, so improving it is the first lever; if it already explained the tool's advantage and Grep was still chosen, a CLAUDE.md instruction would come next.
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the main signal for tool selection. When an agent prefers a built-in like Grep over a more capable MCP tool, enhance the MCP tool's description first.

eli5.question: A smarter search tool exists, but the reviewer keeps using plain Grep. What do you try first? The clue is: the tool's description reads only "Find usages."
eli5.answer: Think of two drawers in a workshop. One says "Hammer". The other says only "Tools", though it holds a much better nail gun. People grab the hammer. The tool description is the drawer label, and it's the main thing Claude reads when it picks a tool. Write what the MCP tool finds that Grep misses, and when to use it. Rule: if a better tool is ignored, fix its description first.
options: Runner-up. A note on the wall helps, but the drawer label is read first and this one says almost nothing.
A redirect hook has to guess which Grep searches are about callers, and it blocks real text searches.
Correct. A clear label tells Claude why and when this tool beats Grep.
A better name helps a little, but a name can't say everything the description should.

deep.premise: You'd think if Claude ignores a tool, you should tell it to use it, or take the alternative away. But Claude picks tools mainly from their descriptions. A two-word description gives no reason to prefer it over a familiar built-in. Fix the primary signal before adding secondary ones.

questions.question: Developers dismiss most of the reviewer's performance findings. The prompt's only guidance for the category is "flag performance problems". Last month the team added "report only findings you are highly confident about". The dismissal rate did not change. The team wants to keep the category, since real performance bugs have reached production. What should they change next?

options.t: Replace that guidance with concrete conditions, such as a query run inside a loop over fetched rows.
options.why: Correct. Categorical criteria tell the reviewer exactly what counts. Vague wording plus a confidence plea does not.

options.t: Add three sample findings to the prompt, each with the flagged code and the reasoning for flagging it.
options.why: Runner-up. Examples are the best tool when written criteria exist but are applied inconsistently. Here there are no criteria yet, so examples would have nothing to illustrate.

options.t: Switch off the performance category until its precision improves, then bring it back.
options.why: Incorrect. Pausing a noisy category protects trust, but the team wants to keep catching real performance bugs.

options.t: Add a confidence score to each finding and post only the ones that score above a set threshold.
options.why: Incorrect. Self-reported confidence is the same lever as the failed "highly confident" line, in numeric form.

questions.decider: The category has no definition, only "flag performance problems," so explicit criteria come first; if written criteria existed and were applied inconsistently, examples would win.
questions.explanation: Vague instructions plus "be conservative" or "only high-confidence" wording do not raise precision. Define the category with concrete, checkable conditions; use few-shot to sharpen consistency once criteria exist.

eli5.question: The performance findings are mostly noise, and asking for confidence didn't help. What next? The clue is: the prompt's only guidance is "flag performance problems."
eli5.answer: Think of telling a new inspector "report anything unsafe". You get a hundred notes. Saying "only report what you're sure about" barely helps. Giving a checklist does: "a loose railing, a blocked exit". For code review, that checklist is explicit criteria, like "a database query inside a loop over results". Rule: define what counts; don't ask for confidence.
options: Correct. A concrete checklist tells the reviewer what to flag.
Runner-up. Examples help once a checklist exists. Without one, they show cases but don't define the line.
Pausing the category would stop the noise, but also the real bugs the team wants caught.
A confidence number is the same "be sure" request that already failed.

deep.premise: You'd think false positives come from the model being too eager, so you ask it to be careful. But the real problem is that nobody told it what a performance problem is. Precision comes from categorical criteria. Confidence wording has already been shown not to help.

questions.trap: More context or reasoning instead of structure
questions.question: The reviewer's dead-code rule says code is not dead if any feature flag can turn it on. Flags in this repository take many forms, from config lookups to annotations and environment checks. New forms appear as teams adopt new libraries. The reviewer honours the rule for some forms and flags the rest as dead. What should the team add to the prompt first?

options.t: A complete list of the flag forms in use today, with the exact call or annotation for each one.
options.why: Runner-up. An exhaustive list works when the set of forms is small and stable. Here new forms keep appearing, so the list would always be behind.

options.t: A line telling the reviewer to treat any flag-guarded code as live unless it is certain otherwise.
options.why: Incorrect. It restates the rule the reviewer already has, with a confidence condition that does not change behaviour.

options.t: A second pass in a fresh instance that rechecks each dead-code finding before it is posted.
options.why: Incorrect. An independent reviewer applies the same rule with the same blind spot about unfamiliar flag forms.

options.t: Three or four worked cases using different flag forms, each giving the verdict and its reason.
options.why: Correct. Varied examples with reasoning teach the pattern, so the reviewer generalises to forms it has not seen.

questions.decider: New flag forms keep appearing, so examples that teach the pattern beat a list of today's forms; if the forms were a small fixed set, listing them would win.
questions.explanation: The rule is clear; the reviewer fails to recognise unfamiliar cases. Few-shot examples that show reasoning help the model generalise to novel patterns, which an enumerated list cannot do.

eli5.question: The rule is fine, but the reviewer misses some kinds of feature flags. What should go in the prompt? The clue is: new flag forms appear as teams adopt new libraries.
eli5.answer: Think of teaching a child to spot dogs. You could list every breed, but new breeds turn up. Showing a few very different dogs and saying why each is a dog teaches the idea. Few-shot examples with reasoning do the same: Claude learns the pattern and spots flag forms it has never seen. Rule: when cases keep changing shape, teach with varied examples, not a list.
options: Runner-up. A full list works if the kinds of flags never change. Here new ones keep arriving.
This repeats the rule with "unless certain", which doesn't help it recognise new flag types.
A second reviewer has the same blind spot about unfamiliar flags.
Correct. Varied worked cases teach the idea so it generalises.

deep.premise: You'd think a precise rule that is still misapplied needs more precise wording, maybe a full list. But the rule is already right. The model fails to recognise some instances of it. When instances keep changing shape, a list goes stale; examples with reasoning teach the underlying pattern.

questions.question: The weekly dependency-risk report sends one synchronous request per module on Saturday night. Nobody reads it until the Monday planning meeting. Each request carries the module's whole source tree, but the report uses only its build file and lockfile. The report must rate every module every week. Which TWO changes cut its cost the most while keeping full coverage?

options.t: Skip modules whose build file and lockfile have not changed since the previous week's run.
options.why: Runner-up. A real saving, and fine if unchanged modules could reuse last week's rating. The report must rate every module weekly, and new advisories can hit unchanged lockfiles.

options.t: Submit the requests through the Message Batches API, with each module's path as its custom_id.
options.why: Correct. Nobody needs the results before Monday, so the 50% batch discount costs nothing in practice; custom_id matches results to modules.

options.t: Merge the modules into a few large requests, each covering one whole product area.
options.why: Incorrect. Fewer, bigger requests spread attention across many modules and lower the quality of each rating.

options.t: Send each module's dependency manifests alone and leave its application source out.
options.why: Correct. Most tokens are source the report never uses. Trimming input to what matters cuts cost without losing coverage.

questions.decider: Results aren't read until Monday and the report reads only manifests, so batching and trimming both fit; if unchanged modules could keep last week's rating, skipping them would also qualify.
questions.explanation: Latency-tolerant work like a weekly report fits the Message Batches API. Sending only the content the task uses cuts tokens. Neither reduces coverage, unlike skipping work.

eli5.question: A weekly report is too expensive. Which two changes save the most but still rate every module? The clues are: nobody reads it until Monday, and the report uses only the build file and lockfile.
eli5.answer: Think of posting parcels. If nobody needs them until Monday, use the cheap slow service (the Message Batches API: half price, up to 24 hours). And don't ship the whole house when only two letters are needed: send just the manifests (trim the input). Skipping some parcels would be cheapest of all, but every module must be rated. Rule: batch work nobody waits for, and send only what the task reads.
options: Runner-up. Skipping saves money but breaks "rate every module every week"; a new advisory can affect an unchanged lockfile.
Correct. Half price, and Monday is plenty of time. custom_id links each result to its module.
Bundling many modules into one request spreads Claude's attention thin.
Correct. Most of each request is source code the report doesn't use.

deep.premise: You'd think the biggest saving must be doing less work, like skipping unchanged modules. But the requirement is full coverage every week. The savings that keep coverage are paying less per request (batch) and sending fewer tokens per request (trim the input).

questions.question: The autofix job patches failing builds. When a patch does not compile, the job reruns Claude with the message "The patch failed. Try again." Most second attempts fail the same way. The compiler output names each broken file, line and error. Every needed fix lies within the repository's own code. Which change best raises the fix rate?

options.t: On each retry, include the compiler's error lines for the failed patch with the original request.
options.why: Correct. The errors are specific and fixable from the repository, so feeding them back gives the retry what it needs.

options.t: After one failed retry, open a draft pull request with the patch and build log for a developer.
options.why: Runner-up. A hand-off is right when the fix needs information the job cannot reach. Here every fix lies in the repository, and the retry carried no feedback yet.

options.t: Run an independent review instance on each failed patch, and pass its comments into the retry.
options.why: Incorrect. It adds feedback, but a reviewer's opinion is weaker than the compiler's exact errors, which already exist.

options.t: On each retry, attach the current contents of every file the failed patch touched.
options.why: Incorrect. More context, but it omits the one thing that says what broke: the compiler's messages.

questions.decider: The compiler names each error and every fix lies within the repo, so retrying with that feedback works; if the fix needed information absent from the repository, routing to a person would win.
questions.explanation: Retries succeed when they carry the specific validation errors and the information exists in the source. A bare "try again" gives the model nothing new; absent information calls for a human instead.

eli5.question: Retries keep failing the same way. How do you make them work? The clue is: the compiler names each error, and every fix lies within the repository's own code.
eli5.answer: Think of a teacher handing back an essay marked only "wrong, redo it". The student repeats the mistake. Circle the errors and they fix them. Retry with error feedback means sending the compiler's exact messages with the retry. This works because the fix is findable in the repo. If it needed a missing password, no feedback would help, and a person should take over. Rule: retry with the specific errors when the fix is reachable.
options: Correct. Give the retry the exact errors.
Runner-up. A developer is the right call when the fix needs something outside the repo. Not here, and the retry hasn't had real feedback yet.
A reviewer's guesses are weaker than the compiler's exact errors.
Re-sending the files gives context, but not what went wrong.

deep.premise: You'd think repeated failure means the job has hit its limit and needs a human. But look at what the retry received: nothing new. A retry only helps if it carries specific feedback, and only if the needed information exists where the model can reach it.

questions.question: After the autofix job's patch compiles, the same session is asked to check the patch for side effects. It approves nearly every patch. Several approved patches later broke callers in other modules. The check's prompt already lists the kinds of side effect to look for. Which change best improves this check?

options.t: Add worked examples of patches that broke callers, each with the clue the check should catch.
options.why: Runner-up. Examples sharpen a reviewer that misses a category. They would be next if the check already ran independently. A session reviewing its own work keeps its original reasoning.

options.t: Turn on extended thinking for the check, and ask it to trace each changed signature step by step.
options.why: Incorrect. Longer reasoning in the same session tends to confirm the patch it just wrote.

options.t: Run the check as a fresh claude -p call that sees the patch and the code but not the fixing session.
options.why: Correct. An independent instance has no stake in the earlier reasoning and catches what self-review misses.

options.t: Give the check a required side_effects array in its output schema for every changed function.
options.why: Incorrect. A schema shapes the report; a session reviewing its own patch fills it with "none" just as readily.

questions.decider: The check runs in the same session that wrote the patch, so an independent instance comes first; if the check were already independent and missed this pattern, examples would win.
questions.explanation: A model reviewing its own work in the same session keeps its generation reasoning and rarely questions it. An independent instance without that history catches more than self-review, extended thinking or examples.

eli5.question: The checker approves nearly everything, and broken patches slip through. What helps most? The clue is: the same session that wrote the patch is asked to check it.
eli5.answer: Think of proofreading your own essay right after writing it. You read what you meant, not what you wrote. A friend who wasn't there spots the mistakes. An independent review instance is that friend: a fresh claude -p call that sees the patch but not the reasoning behind it. Rule: don't let the writer check its own work in the same session.
options: Runner-up. Good examples sharpen a fresh reviewer. The author checking its own work stays blind either way.
Thinking longer in the same session mostly re-confirms its own patch.
Correct. A fresh pair of eyes, with no memory of writing the patch.
A required field gets filled with "no side effects" by the same confident author.

deep.premise: You'd think a reviewer that misses things needs better instructions or more thinking time. But this reviewer is the author. It keeps the reasoning that produced the patch and reads the code through it. The fix is a different reader, not a better prompt for the same one.

questions.question: Many certificates print no deductible at all. The schema marks deductible as a required number. For these certificates the model returns 0 or copies the limit. Either value then posts as if it had been printed. Account assistants cannot tell these values from real ones. Which change best stops these invented values?

options.t: Keep the field required, and have the model enter -1 as a marker whenever no deductible is printed.
options.why: Incorrect. A sentinel number is still a number: downstream code must know the convention, and -1 can be posted as a real value.

options.t: Make deductible nullable in the schema, and describe in the field when to return null.
options.why: Correct. A required number forces the model to invent one. A nullable field gives it an honest way to report "not printed".

options.t: Add two worked certificates with no printed deductible to the prompt, each with its expected output.
options.why: Runner-up. Examples reduce extraction hallucination and would be the fix if the field were already optional. While the schema demands a number, there is no valid output to show.

options.t: Add a deductible_status enum, printed or not_printed, beside the number, and route not_printed.
options.why: Incorrect. It labels the gap, but the required number still forces an invented value into the record.

questions.decider: The schema requires a number for a value that is often absent, so making it nullable is the fix; if the field were already optional and the model still filled it, worked examples would win.
questions.explanation: Required fields push the model to fabricate when the source lacks the value. Optional or nullable fields, with a description saying when to leave them empty, prevent that fabrication.

eli5.question: The model invents a deductible when none is printed. How do you stop it? The clue is: the schema marks deductible as a required number.
eli5.answer: Think of a form that won't submit until every box is filled. If the box asks for your middle name and you have none, you scribble something. The required field is that box. Making it nullable adds "none" as a valid answer. Examples alone can't help while the form still rejects a blank. Rule: if a value can be absent, let the schema say so.
options: A made-up marker number is still a number in the record, and someone has to remember what it means.
Correct. Let the box be empty when nothing is printed.
Runner-up. Examples help once a blank is allowed. While the box is required, there's no right answer to show.
A status flag beside a required box still leaves a guess in the box.

deep.premise: You'd think the model is hallucinating, so you teach it better with examples. But the schema is making it guess: a required number has no valid way to say "not printed". Fix the structure first. Examples are the next lever if it still fills an optional field.

Most retries fail again. In sampled failures both dates are printed clearly, and the model has put each date in the other's field. Which change best fixes these failures?

options.t: Swap the two dates in post-processing whenever the expiry date is earlier than the effective date.
options.why: Incorrect. It hard-codes a guess about the cause and would also flip any genuine misprint, posting it as fact.

options.t: Send any document that fails the date check straight to the account assistants' review queue.
options.why: Runner-up. Hand-off is right when the information is missing or illegible, where retries can't help. Here both dates are printed clearly.

options.t: Resend with the check's details: the two fields, the values returned and the rule they broke.
options.why: Correct. The information is in the document and the error is a mapping mistake, so specific feedback lets the retry correct it.

options.t: Add worked certificates to the prompt showing where several carriers print their two dates.
options.why: Incorrect. With some sixty carriers, a few examples cover few layouts; the specific error is already known per document.

questions.decider: Both dates are printed clearly, so a retry with the specific error can fix the mapping; if the dates were missing or illegible, routing to a person would win.
questions.explanation: Validation-retry loops work when the retry names the specific error and the information exists in the source. Generic retry messages fail; absent information should go to a person.

If they were smudged, a person should look instead. Rule: name the exact error on retry when the answer is in the document.
options: Swapping blindly also flips real misprints and posts them as correct.

Each document needs one extraction call and no other tools. Brokers keep using the live pipeline for new certificates meanwhile. Which approach best fits this re-extraction?

options.why: Incorrect. Batch is the right channel, but the Batches API does not support multi-turn tool calling, and the document needs no tool anyway.

options.t: Submit the archive as Message Batches, one certificate per request, with its ID as custom_id.

options.t: Have a coordinator spawn parallel extraction subagents, several per response, across the archive.

options.t: Send the archive through the live pipeline in nightly chunks, resubmitting failures by document ID.
options.why: Incorrect. Sensible chunking and targeted resubmits, but at full real-time price for work with days of slack.

questions.decider: Results are due next week and each document is one call with no tools, so the Batches API fits; if results were needed within hours, parallel subagents would win.
questions.explanation: The Message Batches API gives 50% savings for latency-tolerant work with no multi-turn tool use, matched by custom_id. Real-time parallelism is for work someone is waiting on.

questions.question: The extraction agent runs in a loop with two lookup tools. The loop ends when Claude's reply contains the phrase "EXTRACTION COMPLETE". Sometimes Claude writes that phrase while also requesting a tool call, and the loop exits before the tool runs. Other runs never write the phrase and stop at an iteration cap. How should the loop decide when to stop?

options.t: Have Claude return a structured status field, and stop when it reads complete with no tool call pending.
options.why: Runner-up. Structured fields beat free-text parsing, and this covers the pending-tool case. But it is still model content acting as the stop signal; the API already reports why each turn ended.

options.t: Keep the phrase, but run any requested tools first and stop on the turn after they return.
options.why: Incorrect. It patches one failure but keeps text parsing as the stop, and runs that skip the phrase still hit the cap.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that ends the loop once every required schema field has a value.
options.why: Incorrect. Code-driven, but it stops on a pre-set condition: the model may still be verifying or correcting values.

options.t: Continue while stop_reason is tool_use, and end the loop when it is end_turn.
options.why: Correct. The stop reason is the API's own signal: run the requested tools and continue, or finish.

questions.decider: The loop is reading Claude's text to decide termination, so it should switch to stop_reason; a structured done flag would only win if no API stop signal existed.
questions.explanation: The agentic loop continues while stop_reason is tool_use and ends on end_turn. Parsing text for completion phrases and relying on iteration caps are named anti-patterns.

eli5.question: The loop stops at the wrong time. What should decide when it ends? The clue is: it looks for a phrase in Claude's reply, and sometimes the phrase appears while a tool call is still pending.
eli5.answer: Think of a phone call where you hang up when the other person says "that's all", even mid-sentence. Better to wait for the call to actually end. The API tells you why each turn ended: stop_reason. If it's tool_use, run the tool and keep going. If it's end_turn, Claude is done. Rule: let stop_reason run the loop, not words in the reply.
options: Runner-up. A status field is tidier than a phrase and checks for pending tools, but it's still Claude's words deciding. The API already says when it's done.
Running tools before obeying the phrase fixes one case; runs without the phrase still hit the cap.
Stopping when all fields are filled can cut Claude off while it is still checking its work.
Correct. Follow the API's stop signal.

deep.premise: You'd think the problem is a fragile phrase, so a cleaner signal like a boolean fixes it. But any signal written by the model is content, and content can say "done" while a tool call is still pending. The API already reports why each turn ended. The loop should follow stop_reason.

Use it?
Why

No, not as the main stop

questions.question: Some submissions hold a broker's cover email plus several certificates. The coordinator reads the email, which names the client and the locations each certificate covers. It then spawns one subagent per certificate with the instruction "Extract this certificate." Subagents often assign certificates to the wrong location. A subagent receives only its certificate. Which change best fixes this?

options.t: Add the client name and the location list from the email to each subagent's task prompt.
options.why: Correct. Subagents don't inherit the coordinator's context, so what they need must be written into their own prompt.

options.t: Give subagents a scoped get_cover_email tool, and tell them to call it before extracting.
options.why: Runner-up. A limited cross-role tool suits frequent, unpredictable lookups. Here the coordinator already holds the exact facts, so passing them is simpler and certain.

options.t: Add the client and the location list from the email to the coordinator's system prompt.
options.why: Incorrect. Right facts, wrong agent. Subagents don't see the coordinator's system prompt.

options.t: Have subagents return a location guess, and let the coordinator check it against the email.
options.why: Incorrect. Coordinator-side checking catches the field after the fact; the rest was still extracted without context.

questions.decider: The coordinator already has the client and location facts and subagents get only their certificate, so the facts go in the subagent prompt; if subagents needed varied, unpredictable lookups, a scoped fetch tool would win.
questions.explanation: Subagents have isolated context and inherit nothing automatically. The coordinator must pass the facts a subagent needs explicitly in its prompt.

eli5.question: Subagents get the location wrong. What fixes it? The clue is: the coordinator has read the email, but each subagent receives only its certificate.
eli5.answer: Think of a manager who reads a client's letter, then hands a temp a single invoice with "process this". The temp never saw the letter. Write the key facts on the task note. Subagents start with an empty desk: they don't see the coordinator's context. The coordinator must put the client and locations into each subagent's prompt. Rule: a subagent knows only what you put in its prompt.
options: Correct. Write the facts the subagent needs into its brief.
Runner-up. A fetch tool is handy for frequent, unpredictable needs. Here the manager already has the facts in hand.
Telling the manager more doesn't help the temp, who never sees the manager's notes.
Checking afterwards fixes one field; the rest was done without the context.

deep.premise: You'd think a subagent spawned by the coordinator shares what the coordinator knows. It doesn't. Subagents start with isolated context. Anything they need must be passed explicitly in the prompt. The coordinator here holds the exact facts, so it should hand them over.

questions.question: The agent calls verify_carrier to check a carrier against the licensing registry, then post_certificate to send results onward. One session handles several certificates in turn. Sometimes the agent posts a certificate without verifying its carrier first. Compliance requires that no certificate from an unverified carrier is ever posted. Which change meets this requirement?

options.t: Make a verification ID from verify_carrier a required input field in post_certificate's schema.
options.why: Incorrect. A schema shapes the call but checks nothing: the model can fill the field without a successful verification.

options.t: Set tool_choice to force verify_carrier on each session's first request, then return to auto.
options.why: Runner-up. Forcing a first tool is right when one call must lead a single-item session. Here each of several certificates needs its own check, and later turns are unforced.

options.t: Add a hook that rejects post_certificate unless verify_carrier has passed for that carrier.
options.why: Correct. A programmatic gate checks every post, for every certificate, regardless of what the model decides.

options.t: Set tool_choice to any on every turn, with verify_carrier described as the step before posting.
options.why: Incorrect. "any" forces some tool call, not the right one; order still rests on the description.

questions.decider: One session posts several certificates and compliance is absolute, so a code gate on every post is needed; if each session handled one certificate, forcing verify_carrier first via tool_choice would suffice.
questions.explanation: When compliance must be deterministic, block downstream tool calls in code until prerequisites complete. Prompts and examples are probabilistic; forced tool_choice only shapes a single request.

eli5.question: The agent sometimes posts without verifying the carrier. What makes that impossible? The clues are: one session handles several certificates, and compliance says this must never happen.
eli5.answer: Think of a ticket barrier. A sign saying "show your ticket" works most of the time. A barrier that only opens for a valid ticket works every time, for every passenger. A programmatic gate is the barrier: code that refuses post_certificate until that carrier is verified. Forcing the first tool call only checks the first passenger. Rule: if it must never happen, enforce it in code on every call.
options: A required field can be filled without the check having passed.
Runner-up. Forcing the first call checks the first certificate. The next ones in the session aren't covered.
Correct. A barrier that checks every post.
"any" makes Claude call a tool, not the right tool first.

deep.premise: You'd think forcing the verify tool with tool_choice is enforcement. It is, but only for the request you set it on. A session that posts several certificates needs the check before each post. Only a gate in code that inspects every post call covers that.

questions.question: The team wants to send only doubtful fields to account assistants and post the rest directly. Accuracy was measured on a uniform random sample and is high overall. Scans from small carriers are rare in that sample. Compliance wants error rates measured for each document type before anything skips review. Which TWO steps together achieve this?

options.t: Have the model report a confidence for each field, and send fields under a fixed cutoff to review.
options.why: Runner-up. Per-field routing is the right shape, but uncalibrated self-reported confidence is unreliable. Calibrated against labelled data, it becomes the answer.

options.t: Label a new sample with a quota per document type, including enough small-carrier scans.
options.why: Correct. Stratified sampling gives each document type enough labelled cases to measure its own error rate.

options.t: Label a larger uniform sample, and report accuracy for each field across all documents.
options.why: Incorrect. Per-field figures are useful, but a uniform sample still under-represents rare types and pools them with the rest.

options.t: Calibrate each field's confidence against the labelled set, and send fields under their cutoff to review.
options.why: Correct. Calibrated field-level confidence decides which individual fields are doubtful and go to a person.

questions.decider: Compliance needs per-type error rates and the team routes individual fields, so stratified sampling plus calibrated field-level confidence fits; uncalibrated self-reported confidence would only do if it had been validated against labelled data.
questions.explanation: Aggregate accuracy hides weak document types. Stratified sampling measures each type; field-level confidence calibrated on labelled data routes individual fields to review.

eli5.question: The team wants to auto-post confident fields and review doubtful ones, safely. Which two steps? The clues are: small-carrier scans are rare in the sample, and compliance wants error rates per document type.
eli5.answer: Think of tasting soup from a big pot by taking random spoonfuls: you rarely taste the bits at the bottom. A stratified sample takes set spoonfuls from each layer, so rare scans get measured. Then you need a way to spot a doubtful value: field-level confidence, checked against labelled answers so its scores mean something. One measures, the other routes. Rule: measure by type, route by calibrated field confidence.
options: Runner-up. Right idea, routing by field, but the model's own confidence isn't trustworthy until checked against real answers.
Correct. Guarantees enough rare scans to measure them.
Per-field numbers from a random sample still bury the rare scans.
Correct. Calibrated scores decide which fields are doubtful.

deep.premise: You'd think high overall accuracy means it's safe to automate. But an aggregate can hide a weak type, especially a rare one barely present in the sample. You need two things: a measurement per document type, and a routing signal per field. Stratified sampling gives the first; calibrated field confidence gives the second.

questions.question: Account assistants check flagged certificates against the source PDF. Policy schedules run to dozens of pages. Most of each review is spent hunting for where a value was printed. The extraction output holds the values and nothing else. Assistants do not need the model's reasoning, only the place to look. Which change most speeds up these reviews?

options.t: Return each value with the page number and the exact span of text it was read from.
options.why: Correct. Source location and quoted text let the assistant jump straight to the evidence.

options.t: Return a calibrated confidence per field, and open the review on the lowest-scoring fields first.
options.why: Runner-up. Calibrated confidence helps decide which fields to check first. The time is lost finding where each value came from, which a score does not tell.

options.t: Highlight in the PDF viewer every place where each extracted value's text appears.
options.why: Incorrect. Close, but common values such as limits repeat across a schedule, so the assistant still has to work out which match was used.

options.t: Return the values grouped under the schedule's own section headings, in document order.
options.why: Incorrect. It narrows the search to a section, but sections span pages; the exact place is still unknown.

questions.decider: The time goes into finding where each value was printed, so per-value source location wins; if the time went into choosing which fields to check, confidence ordering would win.
questions.explanation: Keep a structured mapping from each extracted value to its source location. Provenance lets a reviewer verify quickly; scores and reasoning do not show where to look.

eli5.question: Reviews are slow because assistants hunt through long PDFs. What helps most? The clue is: most of the time is spent finding where a value was printed.
eli5.answer: Think of a textbook answer key that says "42" versus one that says "42, see page 17, line 3". The second lets you check in seconds. Returning the page and quoted text for each value is provenance (a value-to-source mapping). Rule: if people verify extracted values, give them the source location for each one.
options: Correct. Page and exact text point straight to the evidence.
Runner-up. Scores tell you which fields to check first, not where to find them.
Highlighting every match helps, but the same amount often appears in several places.
Knowing the section narrows the hunt but doesn't end it.

deep.premise: You'd think slow review means reviewers need help deciding what to check, so you add confidence scores. But the stem says the time goes into finding each value. That needs a link from value to source: page and quoted text. Provenance, not prioritisation.
